title: The Cost Of Classically Simulating Quantum Communication Is As High As It Could Be
authors: Riccardo Castellano, Pavel Sekatski, Nicolas Brunner
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A long-standing open question is to characterize the classical communication cost of simulating the correlations arising from measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems. We consider this question in the prepare-and-measure scenario. First we construct a classical simulation model involving a finite average number of bits of one-way communication that simulates exactly the correlations arising from arbitrary [MATH]-dimensional quantum states and arbitrary measurements. Second, we show that no classical simulation protocol involving a finite average message dimension can exist for [MATH], hence strengthening a recent result of de Gois, Santos and Vieira. Our first result relies on a more general simulation theorem which can be applied to certain continuous variable (i.e. infinite-dimensional) quantum systems, and even beyond quantum theory, e.g. to generalized probabilistic theories. In particular, we show that multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Overall, our results show that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be.
tldr: This paper shows that classically simulating quantum communication in the prepare-and-measure scenario requires an essentially maximal amount of classical communication, with matching simulation protocols for finite-dimensional and Gaussian continuous-variable systems.
motivation: Characterizing the classical communication cost needed to reproduce quantum correlations is a long-standing open problem with implications for quantum communication complexity and the boundary between quantum and classical information processing.
method: The authors construct explicit classical simulation protocols with a finite average number of one-way communication bits for arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum states and measurements, and prove an impossibility result for finite average message dimension in certain cases, using a general simulation theorem applicable to continuous-variable quantum systems and generalized probabilistic theories.
result: They show that any finite-dimensional quantum prepare-and-measure correlations can be simulated with finite average bits, while for a specific dimension no finite-dimensional classical message can exactly simulate them, and multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy with general Gaussian measurements admit exact finite-bit classical simulation.
conclusion: Thus the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be, establishing tight fundamental limits.

As a notable application, they show that multimode Gaussian states with bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Second, they prove a no-go result: for dimension d ≥ 4, no classical simulation protocol with finite average message dimension can exist. This strengthens a recent result by de Gois, Santos, and Vieira, which ruled out finite communication for d ≥ 5. Together, these results imply that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially maximal, highlighting a stark separation between quantum and classical resources in the prepare-and-measure scenario.

title: Instability Of Markov Chains Under Infinitesimal Coherent Dissipation
authors: Amir-Reza Negari, Yijian Zou, Timothy H. Hsieh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under local Lindbladian evolution, the growth of conditional mutual information and its associated Markov length scale is not limited by Lieb-Robinson bounds, yet it has been unclear how quickly the Markov length can increase. We show that an arbitrarily short, strictly local Lindbladian can generate infinite Markov length from a product state. We also construct strictly local Lindbladians that converge rapidly to steady states with algebraically decaying conditional mutual information. Despite their long-range conditional correlations, the states we construct are local reversibly connected to a product state by sublinear depth circuits. Thus infinite Markov length does not imply slow relaxation nor obstruct phase stability when suitably defined.
tldr: An arbitrarily short local Lindbladian can generate infinite Markov length from a product state, and such long-range conditional correlations do not necessarily imply slow relaxation or phase instability.
motivation: Understanding how quickly conditional mutual information and Markov length can grow under local dissipative dynamics is crucial for characterizing mixed-state phases and the limitations of Lieb-Robinson bounds.
method: The authors construct strictly local Lindbladians and analyze the resulting steady states and their conditional mutual information, using circuit complexity and Markov chain properties.
result: They show that infinitesimal coherent dissipation can produce infinite Markov length from a product state, and construct rapidly relaxing steady states with algebraically decaying CMI that are still reversibly connected to a product state by sublinear-depth circuits.
conclusion: Infinite Markov length is not a fundamental obstacle to fast relaxation or phase stability, broadening the understanding of mixed-state quantum phases under dissipation.

The authors demonstrate that an arbitrarily short, strictly local Lindbladian can generate infinite Markov length from an initial product state, meaning that the CMI does not decay exponentially with distance but instead exhibits long-range correlations. They further construct strictly local Lindbladians that converge rapidly to steady states with algebraically decaying CMI, showing that long-range conditional correlations can coexist with fast relaxation. Despite the infinite Markov length, the resulting states are shown to be local reversibly connected to a product state by sublinear-depth circuits, implying that such long-range correlations do not necessarily imply slow relaxation or obstruct phase stability when suitably defined. The work challenges conventional wisdom that links long-range correlations to slow dynamics and provides explicit counterexamples within the framework of open quantum systems.

Construction of strictly local Lindbladians that converge rapidly to steady states with algebraically decaying conditional mutual information, showing that long-range conditional correlations do not preclude fast relaxation.

Proof that states with infinite Markov length can be local reversibly connected to a product state by sublinear-depth circuits, indicating that such correlations do not obstruct phase stability under suitable definitions.

Explicit counterexamples to the notion that infinite Markov length implies slow relaxation or phase instability, refining the understanding of the relationship between correlation length and dynamics in open systems.

Clarifies the role of Lieb-Robinson bounds in open systems, distinguishing between information propagation and correlation length.

title: Cavity-assisted Dynamic Nuclear Polarisation
authors: Tristan Lorriaux, Yutian Wen, Patrice Bertet, Benjamin Huard, Audrey Bienfait
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic nuclear polarisation transfers polarisation from electron to nuclear spins by relying on a dissipative channel. Here we introduce a cavity-based DNP mechanism which uses the radiative relaxation of the electronic spin through the Purcell effect to bring about the nuclear spin polarisation. We implement this protocol on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins (I=9/2, S=1/2) in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator. A single cycle, combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation, increases a target ground state's population by a factor of [MATH]; a cumulative enhancement of [MATH] is reached with additional cycles, to be compared with the theoretical limit of ninefold set by the degeneracy of the ground manifold. We explain this difference by the competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation on the one hand and a collective effect that slows down the electronic spin radiative decay as the nuclear spin population grows on the other hand. Our results place radiative DNP as an available mechanism at millikelvin temperatures where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen.
tldr: Cavity-assisted dynamic nuclear polarization uses Purcell relaxation of bismuth donor electron spins in silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator to enhance nuclear polarization at millikelvin temperatures.
motivation: Conventional dynamic nuclear polarization relies on phonon-mediated relaxation, which freezes at millikelvin temperatures; an alternative radiative mechanism is needed for low-temperature operation.
method: The authors implement a cavity-based DNP protocol on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator, combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation over single and multiple cycles.
result: A single cycle increases a target ground-state population by a factor, and cumulative cycles yield a polarization enhancement approaching the ninefold degeneracy limit, with deviations explained by competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation and a collective effect that slows radiative decay.
conclusion: Radiative DNP via the Purcell effect is a viable mechanism at millikelvin temperatures where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen, offering a cavity-based route to nuclear spin polarization in hybrid quantum systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a cavity-based dynamic nuclear polarisation (DNP) mechanism that leverages the Purcell effect to transfer polarisation from electron spins to nuclear spins. The protocol is implemented on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins (I=9/2, S=1/2) in isotopically purified silicon, coupled to a superconducting resonator. By combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation, a single cycle enhances the target ground state population by a factor of 1.79±0.04. With additional cycles, a cumulative enhancement of 4.6±0.2 is achieved, compared to the theoretical limit of ninefold set by the degeneracy of the ground manifold. The authors attribute the shortfall to the competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation, as well as a collective effect that slows down the electronic spin radiative decay as nuclear spin population grows. The results establish radiative DNP as a viable mechanism at millikelvin temperatures, where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen.
key_contributions: Introduction of a cavity-based DNP mechanism that uses the Purcell effect for polarisation transfer, distinct from traditional dissipative DNP methods.

Experimental demonstration on bismuth donor spins in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator, achieving a single-cycle enhancement factor of 1.79±0.04 and cumulative enhancement of 4.6±0.2.

Identification and analysis of limiting factors: competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation, and a collective effect that slows electronic spin radiative decay with increasing nuclear polarisation.
Establishment of radiative DNP as an effective mechanism at millikelvin temperatures, where phonon-mediated relaxation is suppressed.

The DNP protocol combines adiabatic microwave pulses (to manipulate electron spins) and radio-frequency pulses (to manipulate nuclear spins) with Purcell relaxation, which transfers polarisation via radiative decay. The use of isotopically purified silicon reduces nuclear spin noise from 29Si, enhancing coherence times. The experiment is performed at millikelvin temperatures to freeze phonon-mediated relaxation, making the Purcell effect the dominant relaxation channel. The cycle is repeated to accumulate nuclear polarisation, and the enhancement is measured by comparing the target ground state population before and after the protocol. The methodology is well-suited for studying spin dynamics in a cavity QED setting, but relies on precise pulse control and low-temperature conditions.
deep_read.results_analysis: The single-cycle enhancement factor of 1.79±0.04 demonstrates the efficacy of the Purcell-based DNP mechanism. With additional cycles, the cumulative enhancement reaches 4.6±0.2, which is about half of the theoretical maximum of 9 (determined by the degeneracy of the ground manifold for I=9/2). The authors explain this gap by two factors: (1) competition between Purcell relaxation and intrinsic relaxation processes that do not contribute to polarisation transfer, and (2) a collective effect where the radiative decay rate of the electronic spin decreases as nuclear polarisation increases, likely due to changes in the effective cavity coupling or spin ensemble dynamics. These results are quantitatively supported by measurements of relaxation rates and polarisation buildup, though the exact mechanism of the collective slowdown is not fully elucidated.

Experimental demonstration: The protocol is successfully implemented on a well-characterised system (Bi donors in isotopically purified Si), with clear enhancement factors reported.

Relevance at millikelvin temperatures: The work addresses a regime where traditional phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen, expanding the toolkit for DNP in quantum technologies.
limitations: The achieved enhancement (4.6±0.2) is only about half of the theoretical limit (9), indicating significant room for improvement and incomplete understanding of the limiting mechanisms.
The collective effect that slows electronic spin radiative decay is not fully characterised, and its dependence on experimental parameters (e.g., cavity coupling, spin concentration) remains unclear.
The protocol's reliance on millikelvin temperatures and a superconducting resonator may limit its applicability to systems where such conditions are not feasible.

title: Stabilizer Entropy Cones As Self-dual Slices Of Linear Rank Cones: A Five-party Gap And Dependence On The Local Dimension
authors: Ruifeng Cao Xidan Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement entropies of multipartite pure states satisfy linear inequalities; for stabilizer states, the backbone of quantum error correction, the achievable entropy vectors generate a convex cone. We show that, after a linear lift, the closure of this cone is exactly the self-dual slice of a classical object on one more element than there are parties: the closed cone generated by the rank functions of arrangements of subspaces over [MATH] for a prime local dimension [MATH], and of subgroups of abelian groups of exponent dividing [MATH] in general. This correspondence brings two features of rank inequalities into play. First, the purifier acts as an extra variable: already for five parties the stabilizer cone is strictly smaller than the quantum linear rank cone, with which earlier evidence suggested it might coincide; an explicit six-variable inequality witnesses the gap. Second, the characteristic of the field enters, so the cone depends on the local dimension. It does not for up to four parties. With enough parties, the cone of [MATH] qudits is contained in that of [MATH] qudits if and only if [MATH] divides [MATH], and already for six parties the logical zero state of Steane's code lies outside the stabilizer cone of every odd local dimension. For this last result we show that the seven-variable characteristic-dependent inequalities we checked all follow from Shannon inequalities on the self-dual slice, and instead transfer one of them through a family of subgroups derived from the Fano plane.
tldr: The paper shows that the stabilizer entropy cone for multipartite pure states coincides with a self-dual slice of a linear rank cone, revealing a five-party gap from the quantum linear rank cone and dependence on local dimension.
motivation: Entanglement entropy inequalities for stabilizer states are central to quantum error correction and multipartite entanglement, but the exact cone structure and its relation to classical rank inequalities were unclear.
method: They lift the stabilizer entropy cone to a self-dual slice of the cone generated by rank functions of subspace arrangements over finite fields (or abelian group subgroups), and use rank inequalities, including an explicit six-variable inequality and Fano-plane subgroup transfer.
result: The stabilizer cone is strictly smaller than the quantum linear rank cone already for five parties; it depends on local dimension for six or more parties, with containment iff p divides q, and Steane code logical zero lies outside the stabilizer cone for all odd local dimensions.
conclusion: These findings establish a precise connection between stabilizer entropy cones and classical rank cones, highlighting the role of the purifier and field characteristic in multipartite entanglement entropy constraints.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper establishes a precise connection between the entanglement entropy cones of stabilizer states and classical rank functions of subspace arrangements over finite fields. The authors show that after a linear lift, the closure of the stabilizer entropy cone for multipartite pure states is exactly the self-dual slice of the cone generated by rank functions of arrangements of subspaces over GF(d) for prime local dimension d, and of subgroups of abelian groups of exponent dividing d in general. This correspondence reveals that the purifier acts as an extra variable, leading to a strict separation between the stabilizer cone and the quantum linear rank cone already at five parties, witnessed by an explicit six-variable inequality. Furthermore, the cone depends on the local dimension d, with the cone for Z_d qudits contained in that for Z_{d'} qudits if and only if d divides d', and the logical zero state of Steane's code lies outside the stabilizer cone for every odd local dimension. The authors also show that the seven-variable characteristic-dependent inequalities they checked all follow from Shannon inequalities on the self-dual slice, and they transfer one such inequality through a family of subgroups derived from the Fano plane.

Transfers a characteristic-dependent inequality through a family of subgroups derived from the Fano plane, and shows that the seven-variable inequalities checked follow from Shannon inequalities on the self-dual slice.

They map the entanglement entropy vectors of stabilizer states to rank functions of subspace arrangements over finite fields, using the connection between stabilizer states and linear error-correcting codes. They then analyze the resulting cone using rank inequalities, which are known to characterize such classical cones. To establish the strict separation between the stabilizer cone and the quantum linear rank cone, they construct explicit inequalities, such as a six-variable inequality, and verify its violation by stabilizer states. For the characteristic-dependent results, they use the Fano plane to derive a family of subgroups and transfer inequalities, and they check that certain seven-variable inequalities follow from Shannon inequalities on the self-dual slice. title: Logical Gate Set Tomography
authors: Piper C. Wysocki, Juan Gonzalez de Mendoza, Karl Mayer, Natalie C. Brown, Ciaran Ryan-Anderson, Jalan A. Ziyad, Jordan H. Hines, Daniel G. Hothem, Corey I. Ostrove, Timothy J. Proctor, Kevin C. Young, Robin J. Blume-Kohout, Charles H. Baldwin, Kenneth M. Rudinger
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.
tldr: The paper introduces logical gate set tomography to fully characterize noisy logical operations in a seven-qubit Steane code on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
motivation: Quantum error correction can suppress noise, but predicting computation success requires understanding the form of residual logical noise, not just its overall magnitude.
method: They extend gate set tomography to logical operations, producing self-consistent representations of a universal single-qubit logical gate set and deriving metrics such as gate fidelity, diamond distance, and tests for non-Markovian and coherent errors.
result: On H1 experimental data, logical GST found predominantly Pauli-stochastic errors, no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and weak coherent-error signatures; emulator data revealed stronger non-Markovian and coherent logical errors and enabled error attribution.
conclusion: Logical GST offers a detailed diagnostic tool for logical noise in quantum error correction, linking physical error sources to logical error mechanisms and supporting fault-tolerant design.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper introduces logical gate set tomography (logical GST), a method for fully characterizing the noise affecting logical operations in a quantum error-corrected system. Logical GST extends standard gate set tomography to the logical level, producing detailed representations of noisy logical gates that can be used to extract metrics such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. The authors apply logical GST to a universal single-qubit logical gate set implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code on Quantinuum's System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion processor. They also use Quantinuum's detailed system emulator to generate higher-shot datasets that reveal error mechanisms not visible in the experimental data.

In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected only weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. In contrast, the emulator-generated data with higher shot counts revealed statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. The authors then use logical GST to perform error attribution with the emulator, showing how specific physical error sources (e.g., two-qubit gate errors, single-qubit gate errors, measurement errors) shape logical error mechanisms. This work provides the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, demonstrating the power of logical GST for diagnosing and understanding noise in QEC implementations.

title: Leakage Benchmarking With Decohering Subgroups In The Presence Of Preparation And Measurement Errors
authors: Shawn Geller, Tongyu Zhao, Alex Kwiatkowski, Scott Glancy, Raymond W. Simmonds, Emanuel Knill
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A common problem with physical qubits is that the state can leak outside the computational subspace. To characterize the problem, it is desirable to measure both the leakage probability and the fidelity of gates inside the computational subspace. Randomized benchmarking is a readily accessible method for estimating average gate fidelities and can be modified to account for leakage. However, in the presence of state preparation and measurement errors (SPAM) there are parameter degeneracies, and fidelities and leakage become underdetermined. We study the example of qudits with any number of leakage levels under the assumption of gate-independent noise. We show that randomized benchmarking sequences with leakage level decoherence can be analyzed as a Markov process with noisy classical preparations and measurements. This result generalizes to randomized benchmarking with random gates from an arbitrary group that contains a phase-decohering subgroup. We characterize the parameter degeneracy in inferring the Markov process, preparations and measurements. Based on this characterization we develop a measurement and inference method taking advantage of known conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain fidelity, leakage and other parameters of the Markov process, state preparations and measurements. As part of our study, we experimentally implemented the measurement method for a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmons, for which there are two leakage levels. We determined confidence intervals accounting for parameter degeneracy for a number of performance parameters of the system. For leakage and fidelity, we compare these intervals to those obtained for several conventional methods for leakage benchmarking.
tldr: A new method for benchmarking leakage and gate fidelity in qubits that accounts for state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors by modeling randomized benchmarking as a Markov process with decohering subgroups, experimentally demonstrated on a transmon qubit.
motivation: Leakage outside the computational subspace and SPAM errors cause parameter degeneracies, making it difficult to accurately characterize qubit performance using standard randomized benchmarking.
method: The authors model leakage randomized benchmarking as a Markov process with noisy classical preparations and measurements, characterize the parameter degeneracy, and develop a measurement and inference method that uses conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain fidelity, leakage, and other parameters. They experimentally implement the method for a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmons.
result: They determine confidence intervals for performance parameters and compare them to conventional leakage benchmarking methods, showing that their approach provides more reliable characterization under SPAM errors.
conclusion: The approach generalizes randomized benchmarking with phase-decohering subgroups and offers a robust framework for leakage benchmarking in the presence of SPAM, applicable to superconducting qubits.

title: Dynamical Decoupling Of Nonclassical States In A Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Namit Anand, Rocky Y. Su, Akram Youssry, Ritik Sareen, Jeffrey Marshall, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Danielle Holmes, Benjamin Wilhelm, Bibek Pokharel, Xi Yu, Laura A. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. title: Optimal Disorder Strength For Approximate Unitary $k$-Designs In Spin Chains
authors: Tian-Gang Zhou, Yi-Neng Zhou, Thierry Giamarchi, Julian Sonner
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulators with disordered spin Hamiltonians offer a natural route to Haar-like unitary ensembles, but face a competition. Disorder enhances randomness, yet strong disorder suppresses dynamics and localizes the system in the computational basis. This suggests an optimal intermediate disorder strength for approximating a unitary [MATH]-design, which has so far been identified mainly empirically. Here, we develop a perturbative theory for the moment gap [MATH], the deviation of the [MATH]-th moment operator from its Haar value, for the full spectrum of the interacting XXZ chain in a fixed-magnetization sector. We find the non-monotonic asymptotic scalings [MATH] at weak disorder and [MATH] at strong disorder, whose crossover sets an optimal disorder strength [MATH], where [MATH] is the energy scale of the non-random interaction. We further show that a multi-quench protocol further suppresses the gap exponentially in the number of quenches. Numerical simulations confirm both scalings and this exponential suppression, and we demonstrate the usefulness of the protocol for classical shadow tomography. This work suggests that strong disorder may block both thermalization and the formation of unitary designs through a common localization mechanism.

title: A Modular Quantum Computer Based On Cornucopia Codes
authors: Zhide Lu, Weikang Li, Yinghao Ma, Hanyu Yan, Bingrun Wang, Yixuan Ma, Zheng-Zhi Sun, Dong-Ling Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes can store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.
tldr: Proposes a modular fault-tolerant quantum computer architecture based on Cornucopia codes that enables universal logical operations on many logical qubits with low overhead.
motivation: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes can store many logical qubits in one block, but universal logical operations typically require large ancilla overhead that erodes the encoding-rate advantage.
method: Focuses on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code and uses its translation symmetry to construct reusable gadgets for addressing 1,422 logical qubits per block, with blocks connected by bridges to form a modular universal logical processor.
result: Excluding magic-state factories, a module with enough workspace for the basic instruction set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone.
conclusion: The architecture preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, offering a route toward low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

To achieve this, the authors exploit the translation symmetry of the Cornucopia code to construct a family of reusable gadgets that can individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. title: Stabilizer R\'enyi Entropy Without A Phase Reference
authors: Savan Kharel Jinwei Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer R\'enyi entropy quantifies magic relative to a complete Pauli frame. In settings such as helicity states of massless particles, unsynchronized qubit registers, energy eigenbases, and systems under superselection rules, the computational basis may be fixed while the transverse Pauli axes remain unspecified. The stabilizer R\'enyi entropy then depends on the choice of those axes. We define a phase-averaged stabilizer R\'enyi entropy by averaging the Pauli moments before taking the logarithm. It is exactly invariant under independent local rephasings. For pure states, it vanishes precisely when the state is a stabilizer state in every phase convention. For a broad class of sparse supports, it reduces to a closed-form function of the basis-state probabilities alone. Within this class, the ceiling for [MATH] channels is [MATH] for [MATH] and [MATH] for two channels. We apply the invariant to tree-level gluon scattering at four and five points, where the helicity-basis phases are unspecified. It saturates the two- and three-channel ceilings: [MATH] at four points and [MATH] in [MATH] scattering. In same-helicity [MATH] scattering, it lies between a floor of [MATH] and a ceiling of [MATH], reached in the resolved soft limit and particular collinear limits, respectively. In every configuration studied, the invariant is independent of the fixed external colors.

The SRE is conventionally defined relative to a complete Pauli frame, i.e., a full set of Pauli axes (X, Y, Z) for each qubit. However, in many physical settings—such as helicity states of massless particles, unsynchronized qubit registers, energy eigenbases, and systems under superselection rules—only the computational basis (Z axis) is fixed, while the transverse Pauli axes (X and Y) remain unspecified. The SRE then depends on the arbitrary choice of these transverse axes, making it ill-defined. The authors propose a phase-averaged stabilizer Rényi entropy that averages the Pauli moments over independent local rephasings before taking the logarithm, rendering it exactly invariant under such rephasings. They prove that for pure states, this invariant vanishes precisely when the state is a stabilizer state in every phase convention. For a broad class of sparse supports, they derive a closed-form expression depending only on the basis-state probabilities, and establish upper bounds: for n channels, the ceiling is ln[n^3/(6n-5)] for n≥3 and ln(7/5) for two channels. They apply this invariant to tree-level gluon scattering at four and five points, where helicity-basis phases are unspecified. The invariant saturates the two- and three-channel ceilings: ln(7/5) at four points and ln(27/13) in 3→2 scattering. In same-helicity 2→3 scattering, it lies between a floor of ln(8/7) and a ceiling of ln(184/125), reached in the resolved soft limit and particular collinear limits, respectively. Notably, the invariant is independent of the fixed external colors in all studied configurations.

title: The Generalized Beads Representation: An Informationally Complete Visualization Of Mixed Quantum States
authors: Celina Br\"autigam, Steffen J. Glaser, Dennis Huber
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A deep understanding of quantum information theory is essential for quantum science and technology. However, quantum mechanics and particularly quantum information theory suffer from a lack of intuitive images. Visualization tools offer novel perspectives on many problems in quantum physics by revealing important properties of quantum states and processes that are otherwise obscured by abstract mathematical formalisms. Here, we extend the previously established BEADS representation of pure states to the so-called generalized BEADS representation of mixed quantum states. We introduce spherical functions, so-called beads to visualize correlation structures of mixed quantum states. A recursive optimization scheme is used to obtain minimum-entanglement pure state decompositions of all subsystems of a given N-qubit state. We show how correlation function components can be decomposed into individual contributions that directly correspond to different types of correlations of mixed states. This allows us to visually characterize the total correlation, genuine n-partite entanglement, nonclassical quantum-discord-type correlations as well as classical correlations. After outlining the mathematical details relevant for constructing the representation, we examine the generalized BEADS representations for various classes of mixed states including product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, as well as entangled states. As exemplary applications of the generalized BEADS representation, we showcase entanglement distillation and the effects of noise channels.
tldr: The paper extends the BEADS representation from pure to mixed quantum states, providing an informationally complete visual tool that decomposes correlation functions into contributions from classical, discord-type, and entanglement correlations.
motivation: Quantum information theory lacks intuitive visual representations, especially for mixed-state correlation structures, which are often obscured by abstract formalisms.
method: The authors introduce generalized BEADS using spherical bead functions and a recursive optimization scheme to obtain minimum-entanglement pure-state decompositions for all subsystems, then decompose correlation-function components into distinct correlation types.
result: The representation visually characterizes total correlation, genuine multipartite entanglement, quantum-discord-type nonclassical correlations, and classical correlations for product, classically correlated, separable nonclassically correlated, and entangled mixed states, with applications to entanglement distillation and noise channels.
conclusion: The generalized BEADS representation offers a practical visualization and analysis tool for understanding and distinguishing correlation structures in mixed quantum states.

title: Programmable Polaron Models And Tomography In Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulators
authors: Filip Marijanovic, Utso Bhattacharya, Abhishek Menon, Visal So, Guido Pagano, Eugene Demler
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong coupling between mobile charge carriers or excitons and lattice vibrations gives rise to polarons: quasiparticles formed by charge carriers dressed by a cloud of phonon excitations. Polaron formation determines transport properties of systems ranging from transition-metal oxides and organic semiconductors to light-harvesting complexes. In excitonic systems that admit a hard-core boson description, mapping the excitations to pseudospins provides a natural framework for studying polaron physics, including the nonperturbative regime in which hopping amplitudes, phonon energies, and coupling strengths are comparable. Here, we propose a trapped-ion blueprint for realizing spin-phonon Hamiltonians with programmable spatial coupling between excitation density and phonon displacements, encompassing local Holstein and long-range Fr\"ohlich-type interactions. To access strongly dressed quasiparticles whose bare spectral weight is suppressed, we introduce displaced Green's functions implemented through spin-dependent phonon displacements. Their spectral response reveals the polaron band spectrum, including binding energies and phonon-excitation sidebands, while spatially resolved measurements probe the structure of the phonon dressing cloud, providing a route to polaron tomography. We further complement this spectroscopy with direct and ancilla-assisted measurements of spin-phonon correlations that track the coupled dynamics of the excitation and its environment. These approaches connect the emergent quasiparticle spectrum to the microscopic buildup of its dressing cloud, enabling controlled studies of how the spatial range of coupling shapes polaron formation and mobility.
tldr: A trapped-ion blueprint for programmable spin-phonon Hamiltonians enables simulation of polaron physics and tomographic access to the phonon dressing cloud.
motivation: Polaron formation governs transport in diverse materials, and trapped ions provide a controllable platform to study nonperturbative spin-phonon models where hopping, phonon energy, and coupling are comparable.
method: The authors propose trapped-ion implementations of local Holstein and long-range Fröhlich spin-phonon couplings with programmable spatial dependence, using spin-dependent phonon displacements to realize displaced Green's functions and ancilla-assisted spin-phonon correlation measurements.
result: The protocol yields spectral responses revealing the polaron band, binding energies, and phonon sidebands, while spatially resolved measurements of the phonon dressing cloud enable tomography of the polaron quasiparticle.

title: Beyond The Lemon: Spectra Of Random Lindblad Operators With A Hamiltonian Component
authors: Mykhailo Hontarenko, Wojciech Tarnowski, Sergey Denisov, Karol \.zyczkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generators of continuous-time quantum Markovian evolution, known as Lindblad operators, play a key role in the theory of open quantum systems. The question of how to define and characterize random Lindblad operators has attracted considerable attention in recent years. Purely dissipative random Lindbladians have been extensively studied using toolboxes of free probability and non-Hermitian random matrix theories, which helped, among other results, to uncover a characteristic lemon-like spectral support. In this work, we focus on random Lindbladians with a Hamiltonian component. We analyze three ensembles of increasing complexity, designed to illustrate the joint effects of dissipative and Hamiltonian dynamics. While the first two ensembles allow for an exact analytic treatment with standard probabilistic and free-probability methods, the generic case of independently random Hamiltonian and dissipative components requires a novel framework that combines operator-valued free probability with sequential noise averaging. For this ensemble, our approach preserves the underlying tensor-product structure of the Lindblad operator and derives a general equation for the spectral boundary. We characterize the effect of Hamiltonian-induced spectral squeezing and explain how the spectral support changes with the relative Hamiltonian strength and the rank of the dissipative component.
tldr: This work derives spectral boundaries for random Lindblad operators with a Hamiltonian component, extending the known 'lemon' spectrum of purely dissipative random Lindbladians.
motivation: Random Lindblad operators have been extensively studied for purely dissipative dynamics, but the effect of a Hamiltonian component on their spectra is less understood.
method: The authors analyze three ensembles of increasing complexity, using standard probabilistic and free-probability methods for the first two, and a novel framework combining operator-valued free probability with sequential noise averaging for the generic case.
result: They obtain a general equation for the spectral boundary, characterize Hamiltonian-induced spectral squeezing, and show how the spectral support depends on Hamiltonian strength and dissipative rank.
conclusion: The framework preserves the tensor-product structure of the Lindblad operator and provides a systematic way to understand spectral properties of open quantum systems with both dissipative and Hamiltonian dynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the spectral properties of random Lindblad operators that include both dissipative and Hamiltonian components. The authors study three ensembles of increasing complexity: (i) a purely dissipative ensemble, (ii) a dissipative ensemble with a deterministic Hamiltonian, and (iii) a fully random ensemble where both Hamiltonian and dissipative parts are independently random. The first two ensembles are analytically tractable using standard random matrix theory and free probability, while the third requires a novel combination of operator-valued free probability and sequential noise averaging. The main result is a general equation for the spectral boundary of the random Lindbladian in the complex plane, which reveals a Hamiltonian-induced squeezing effect: as the Hamiltonian strength increases, the spectral support contracts and deforms. The authors also analyze how the spectral support depends on the rank of the dissipative component, providing a comprehensive picture of the interplay between coherent and incoherent dynamics in open quantum systems.

For the first two ensembles, they use standard free probability tools to compute the spectral density and boundary. For the most general ensemble, they develop a new approach that combines operator-valued free probability with sequential noise averaging. This method allows them to handle the tensor-product structure of the Lindblad operator and derive a self-consistent equation for the spectral boundary. The sequential noise averaging technique effectively decouples the Hamiltonian and dissipative parts by averaging over the noise in a stepwise manner, enabling the use of free probability even when the components are independent. The analysis is supported by numerical simulations that confirm the analytical predictions.

title: Quantum Ldpc Codes From Polynomial Minors

abstract: ArXiv:2610.19459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct quantum codes from codewords of a cyclic code and the minors of a polynomial matrix. The construction uses a two-row, three-column matrix whose minors yield a second matrix satisfying the CSS orthogonality condition. We derive the code dimension from the greatest common divisors of the entries and minors, with a simplified formula for odd lifting factors. title: Transport Information Beyond Strong Eigenstate Thermalization
authors: Avadhut V. Purohit, Harshit Sharma, Udaysinh T. Bhosale
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong eigenstate thermalization (ETH) in operationally mean-ergodic, non-chaotic systems provides an opportunity to investigate whether Floquet eigenstates retain information about classical transport beyond their leading thermodynamic behavior. We address this question using the double kicked top (DKT), which exhibits nonmixing transport and dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport under variation of its control parameters. We show that the coefficient [MATH] of the leading finite-size correction to the normalized eigenstate entanglement entropy (EE) [MATH] tracks the restructuring between these transport regimes even when the thermodynamic-limit entropy [MATH] becomes nearly insensitive to them. This coefficient [MATH] is positive for nonmixing transport and negative when dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport dominate. The coefficient's sign reversal in the coexistence regime remains stable as the semiclassical resolution increases. Our results demonstrate that finite-size eigenstate structure can encode signatures of classical transport that are invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy, providing an eigenstate-based diagnostic of dynamical organization beyond the leading thermodynamic behavior associated with strong ETH.

title: Combining Post-Quantum Cryptography And Quantum Key Distribution: Taxonomy, Constructions, Proofs, Standards, Deployments And Open Problems
authors: Mona Alotaibi, Noora Fetais, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) address the quantum threat from opposite directions: PQC replaces vulnerable public-key algorithms with schemes believed to resist quantum cryptanalysis, while QKD derives keys whose secrecy rests on physical assumptions rather than computational ones. Because each approach has a distinct failure mode, a growing body of work combines them so that a session key remains secure if either component holds. We first establish the deployed baseline, hybrid classical-plus-PQC key exchange, against which QKD-augmented designs must be judged. We then propose a taxonomy of hybrid PQC-QKD designs along eight dimensions (integration layer, combiner construction, authentication scope and source, QKD topology, trusted entities, key-delivery interface, classical component, and evidence type), and use it to compare published protocols, including Muckle and its successors, MACsec and TLS integrations, and IKEv2 mechanisms standardised in RFCs 8784, 9370, and 9867. We examine key-combiner constructions in light of the KEM-combiner literature and of NIST, ETSI, and ITU-T guidance, and map the security arguments for hybrid PQC-QKD protocols onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, established guarantee, and limitations. We synthesise deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks, distinguishing the few testbeds that have run PQC in the key path from pure-QKD deployments, and summarise the standards and policy landscape, including the positions of national security agencies that recommend against relying on QKD alone. We close with open problems: authentication of the QKD classical channel, shared-infrastructure threat models, device certification versus formal proofs, formal verification of hybrid handshakes, and the lack of peer-reviewed deployment economics.
tldr: A taxonomy and survey of hybrid post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) designs, covering protocols, security proofs, standards, deployments, and open problems.
motivation: PQC and QKD address the quantum threat from opposite directions and have complementary failure modes, motivating hybrid approaches whose session key remains secure if either component holds.
method: The authors propose an eight-dimension taxonomy to classify hybrid PQC-QKD designs and map their security arguments onto a common grid of security model, assumptions, permitted compromise, guarantee, and limitations.
result: They compare published protocols including Muckle successors and MACsec/TLS/IKEv2 integrations, examine key-combiner constructions against KEM-combiner literature and NIST/ETSI/ITU-T guidance, and synthesize deployment evidence from metropolitan and national QKD networks.
conclusion: The survey summarizes standards and policy positions, noting that some national security agencies recommend against relying on QKD alone, and identifies open problems in authentication, shared-infrastructure threats, certification, formal verification, and deployment economics.

title: A Compact Six-beam 3d Magneto-optical Trap Based On Multifunctional Metasurface Chips
authors: Chen Qing, Huijie Sun, Yize Liu, Yuxuan Liao, Yongzhuo Li, Dengke Zhang, Xue Feng, Yidong Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs), indispensable to cold-atom-based quantum computing and quantum precision measurement, are increasingly desired in compact and stable form. Particularly, the six-beam 3D-MOT, distinguished by symmetric geometry and superior trapping performance, finds particularly broad applications. Conventional implementations, however, rely on complex and bulky free-space optics, hindering miniaturization, practical assembly, and long-term stability. Here, we demonstrate a compact six-beam 3D-MOT system that employs two multifunctional optical metasurface chips to implement the optical-field functionalities required for cooling and trapping atoms. By combining two metasurface chips and a vacuum cell, a photonic-integrated cell module (PICM) is implemented as the core assembly and the volume is only" 73*73*107 mm^3" . In success, 1.3 * 10^3 Rb atoms are trapped and cooled to the temperature of ~183 {\mu}K. It should be noticed that the laser beam is guided to the metasurface through optical fiber, thus such fully fiber-coupled architecture enables straightforward and stable operations. We believe that this work would pave a practical route toward compact and portable 3D-MOT.
tldr: A compact six-beam 3D magneto-optical trap is demonstrated using multifunctional metasurface chips, trapping 1.3e3 Rb atoms at ~183 µK in a fiber-coupled photonic-integrated cell module.
motivation: Cold-atom quantum computing and precision measurement require compact, stable MOT systems, but conventional free-space optics hinder miniaturization and long-term stability.
method: Two multifunctional optical metasurface chips implement the cooling and trapping optical fields, combined with a vacuum cell into a photonic-integrated cell module (73×73×107 mm³) with fiber-coupled laser delivery.
result: 1.3×10^3 Rb atoms are trapped and cooled to a temperature of ~183 µK.
conclusion: This work provides a practical route toward compact and portable 3D-MOTs for cold-atom quantum technologies.

The laser light is delivered to the metasurfaces via optical fibers, enabling a fully fiber-coupled architecture that simplifies assembly and enhances stability. title: Invertible Subalgebras For Chiral Semion Topological Order
authors: Yu-An Chen, Meng Sun, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Zongyuan Wang, Bowen Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chiral topological order is incompatible with strictly two-dimensional local commuting-projector Hamiltonians on finite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert spaces. Invertible subalgebras (ISAs) provide an alternative framework. We construct an ISA supporting chiral semions, together with its anti-semion commutant, on a square lattice with one qubit per edge. We give explicit non-Pauli generators for both algebras and prove that together they generate all local operators on the Hilbert space. Starting from the [MATH] toric code, we condense the boson [MATH] and identify the semion and anti-semion algebras. We then decompose each [MATH] qudit into two qubits and use a finite-depth circuit to disentangle one qubit per edge fixed by the condensation constraints. Pumping the semion ISA along the [MATH] direction defines an explicit three-dimensional non-Clifford quantum cellular automaton (QCA). We show that pumping eight times is equivalent to a translation followed by a finite-depth quantum circuit with ancillary qubits. We also give an explicit finite-depth circuit relating this construction to the semion QCA previously obtained from topological quantum field theory. A similar condensation construction yields a [MATH] ISA on a square lattice. Together with the semion and earlier odd-prime ISAs, finite stacking realizes every pointed Witt class of bosonic Abelian anyon theories. Finally, we extend both constructions to all spatial dimensions [MATH], with one qubit or [MATH] qudit on each [MATH]-cell for the semion or [MATH] ISA, respectively.
tldr: The paper constructs invertible subalgebras that realize chiral semion topological order and uses them to define a non-Clifford quantum cellular automaton, extending the construction to all spatial dimensions.
motivation: Chiral topological order is incompatible with strictly two-dimensional local commuting-projector Hamiltonians, motivating alternative frameworks such as invertible subalgebras to explicitly model chiral anyons and related quantum cellular automata.
method: Starting from the toric code, the authors condense a boson, identify semion and anti-semion subalgebras with explicit non-Pauli generators, decompose qudits into qubits, and pump the semion ISA to obtain a three-dimensional non-Clifford QCA, with condensation and stacking used for higher dimensions and other Witt classes.
result: Explicit generators are given for the semion and anti-semion algebras, pumping eight times is shown to equal a translation followed by a finite-depth circuit, and finite stacking realizes every pointed Witt class of bosonic Abelian anyon theories, with extensions to all spatial dimensions.
conclusion: The invertible subalgebra framework provides a systematic construction of chiral semion topological order and QCA, connecting to topological quantum field theory and classifying Abelian anyon theories, though its direct relevance to the user's core quantum information interests is limited.

title: Federated Unlearning Of Quantum Data Via Classical Shadows
authors: Zihao Ding, Jun Huang, Cong-Cong Xing
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum federated learning trains a quantum neural network (QNN) across nodes that hold quantum data, such as the states of quantum sensors. To forget data, unlearning methods for quantum models replay them, and federated unlearning from stored updates removes whole nodes only. Quantum data cannot be replayed, since a state is consumed when measured and cannot be cloned. We propose Shadow-based Data Erasure (SHADE), in which each node records a classical shadow of every training state, a few randomized single-qubit measurements taken at training time. The gradient and curvature of a QNN on a state are expectations of observables, so SHADE estimates them for the forget data from the shadows at any later parameters and removes their effect by a federated Newton correction. Only classical estimates cross the network. We prove that the shadow size needed for a target unlearning error grows exponentially in the size of the backward light cone of the measured observable and not in the number of qubits. In simulation with 50 nodes and on edge boards, SHADE matches the forget accuracy of retraining within 0.5 points, without replay and in under 0.2 s.
tldr: SHADE enables federated unlearning of quantum data by recording classical shadows at training time and applying a federated Newton correction, avoiding replay of quantum states.
motivation: Quantum data cannot be replayed or cloned, so existing unlearning methods for quantum federated learning are ineffective; forgetting data across nodes is needed.
method: Each node stores classical shadows of training states; from these, gradients and curvature of a QNN are estimated for forget data at later parameters, and a federated Newton correction removes their effect using only classical communication.
result: The required shadow size scales exponentially with the backward light cone size of the measured observable, not the total qubit number; simulations with 50 nodes and edge boards match retraining forget accuracy within 0.5 points in under 0.2 s.
conclusion: Classical shadows provide a practical route to federated unlearning for quantum models without replay, though the exponential light-cone dependence may limit scalability.

title: Quantum Reservoir Computing For Attention-like Selective Reproduction
authors: Christoph Simon Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Choosing which information to use as the context changes is a basic cognitive operation. We introduce a new task of this kind for quantum reservoir computing (QRC): a binary cue indicates which of two simultaneous input streams the reservoir must reproduce. In simulated spin reservoirs with a trained linear readout, infinitely many measurements (exact expectation values) let the reservoir reproduce the cued stream accurately. At a finite number of measurements \(N_M\), the score exceeds that of a linear readout of the raw inputs only at large \(N_M\) because of sampling noise. Performance increases with both entanglement and coherence in the computational basis, and then saturates. These results show that QRC can select and reproduce a cued stream, and they are a starting point for harder cognitive tasks.
tldr: The paper introduces a quantum reservoir computing task where a binary cue selects which of two input streams a spin reservoir must reproduce, showing accurate reproduction with exact expectation values and performance scaling with entanglement and coherence.
motivation: Selective context-dependent information selection is a basic cognitive operation, and the authors aim to extend quantum reservoir computing to such attention-like tasks.
method: They simulate spin reservoirs with a trained linear readout on a binary-cued stream reproduction task, varying the number of measurements and analyzing the roles of entanglement and coherence.
result: With infinite measurements, the reservoir reproduces the cued stream accurately; at finite measurement counts, sampling noise means it only outperforms a linear readout of raw inputs at large N_M, and performance increases with entanglement and coherence before saturating.
conclusion: Quantum reservoir computing can select and reproduce a cued stream, providing a starting point for harder cognitive tasks in quantum machine learning.

title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip For Superconducting Quantum Processor
authors: Rutian Huang, Xiao Geng, Xinyu Wu, Genting Dai, Liangliang Yang, Jianshe Liu, Wei Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.
tldr: The paper proposes a cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) based on adjustable inductors that lets a single microwave cable drive many superconducting qubits via XY control at 20 mK.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors is limited by the large number of microwave control lines required per qubit, so a compact multiplexed cryogenic control solution is needed.
method: The MCC is designed as a non-reciprocal device using adjustable inductors to generate 4–8 GHz signals, and is characterized through frequency-domain (filters, isolators, power splitters, qubit/load impedance) and time-domain (response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude/frequency compensation) simulations.
result: Simulations show the MCC can produce qubit-specific microwave XY drive pulses without crosstalk and be co-packaged with superconducting qubits at the 20 mK stage.
conclusion: The MCC could drastically reduce microwave control wiring, aiding the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processors, though results are simulation-only and hardware-level.

title: Retrieving Metrological Information From Noisy Squeezed Spin States Via Bayesian Optimization
authors: Enze Li, Yunjie Cai, Jingwei Zhang, Emi Yukawa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency inhomogeneity can obscure the metrological advantage of squeezed spin states, making the choice of readout crucial. We study interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and optimize a common collective readout over independent disorder realizations. Using Bayesian optimization of the full measurement-outcome distribution, we identify observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators that yield greater classical Fisher information than the optimized dipole readout considered here. For ensembles of up to 17 spins, their disorder-averaged CFI surpasses the standard quantum limit at both disorder strengths studied, including a regime where the dipole readout remains below it. For the larger ensembles studied, fixing the encoding axis to the direction that maximizes the disorder-averaged quantum Fisher information retains nearly the same performance. These results identify a route to extracting metrological information from frequency-disordered spin ensembles through the choice of collective observable.
tldr: Bayesian optimization identifies collective dipole-quadrupole observables that retrieve metrological information from frequency-disordered squeezed spin ensembles beyond the standard quantum limit.
motivation: Frequency inhomogeneity can obscure the metrological advantage of squeezed spin states, making the choice of readout observable crucial for extracting useful information.
method: The authors model interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and use Bayesian optimization of the full measurement-outcome distribution to find optimal collective observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators, comparing disorder-averaged classical and quantum Fisher information for up to 17 spins.
result: The optimized dipole-quadrupole observables yield greater disorder-averaged classical Fisher information than an optimized dipole readout and surpass the standard quantum limit at both disorder strengths studied, including a regime where the dipole readout remains below it; for larger ensembles, fixing the encoding axis to maximize quantum Fisher information retains nearly the same performance.
conclusion: The choice of collective observable provides a route to extracting metrological information from frequency-disordered spin ensembles and highlights measurement optimization as a practical tool in noisy quantum sensing.

title: The Capacity Of The Noisy Torn Paper Channel And The Noisy Shuffling Channel
authors: Netanel Raviv Junsheng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The torn paper channel breaks a codeword into fragments and returns all fragments without their original order. The noisy torn paper channel additionally introduces bit substitution errors to each fragment. Recovering the message therefore requires accounting for both bit errors and uncertainty about the fragment order. We establish a capacity upper bound for the noisy torn paper channel that matches the achievable rate of Ravi, Vahid, and Shomorony and resolves their conjecture. Our results also determine the capacity of the noisy shuffling channel of Shomorony and Heckel, in which all fragments have the same length, and resolve their open question.
tldr: This paper establishes a capacity upper bound for the noisy torn paper channel and the noisy shuffling channel, matching known achievable rates and resolving open conjectures.
motivation: The torn paper and shuffling channels model data storage and communication where fragments are shuffled and subject to substitution errors, but their fundamental capacity limits were not fully characterized.
method: The authors use information-theoretic and combinatorial techniques to derive upper bounds on the capacity of channels that fragment, permute, and corrupt codewords.
result: The upper bound matches the achievable rate of Ravi, Vahid, and Shomorony for the noisy torn paper channel and determines the capacity of the noisy shuffling channel, resolving their open questions.
conclusion: These results close the capacity characterization for these channels, with implications for coding schemes in DNA storage and related synchronization-error settings.

title: Nonlinear Fixed-distance Codes Via Real Lifts Of Moment Configurations
authors: Sergey Yekhanin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] denote the largest size of a code of length [MATH] and minimum Hamming distance [MATH] over an alphabet of [MATH] symbols. For fixed [MATH] and [MATH] we construct codes with redundancy [MATH] for all large [MATH]. No algebraic structure is imposed on the alphabet, and the codes are not linear. For [MATH] and [MATH] the coefficient of [MATH] matches the Hamming bound, so the redundancy is determined up to lower-order terms. At distance four the codes are provably better than every linear code: by the polynomial-method bound for cap sets, [MATH]-linear codes with [MATH] require a strictly larger coefficient in front of [MATH]. The construction imposes moment checksums over an auxiliary finite field, as BCH codes do, but one fewer than the distance would normally require. The affine-line theorem from prior work describes the dependencies left by these checks. We exclude them by placing the code positions inside a specially structured subset of the field, built from Behrend's sphere construction with the help of algebraic number theory.
tldr: The paper constructs nonlinear fixed-distance classical error-correcting codes via real lifts of moment configurations, achieving redundancy matching the Hamming bound for certain parameters and provably beating all linear codes at distance four.
motivation: Classical coding theory seeks to determine the maximum code size for given length and minimum distance, and to understand whether nonlinear codes can outperform linear ones near fundamental bounds such as the Hamming bound.
method: The construction uses moment checksums over an auxiliary finite field, as in BCH codes, but with one fewer check than the distance normally requires; unwanted dependencies are excluded by placing code positions inside a structured subset of the field built from Behrend's sphere construction with algebraic number theory.
result: For fixed alphabet size and distance, codes with redundancy matching the Hamming bound coefficient are obtained in several cases; at distance four, the codes are strictly better than every linear code, as shown by the polynomial-method bound for cap sets.
conclusion: The work provides new nonlinear codes that surpass linear codes and approach optimal redundancy, using a combination of combinatorial and algebraic number-theoretic techniques.

title: A Boson-informed Neural Network For Ground States Of Many-Body Schr\"{o}dinger Equations
authors: Zhizhong Kong, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Cheng Yuan, Xiaofei Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a symmetry-preserving Boson-informed neural network (BINN) for the variational Monte Carlo computation of interacting-boson ground states in continuous space. The framework explicitly separates the two dominant physical scales of the system. At the microscopic interaction scale, a cell Jastrow factor absorbs the leading near-contact stiffness, while at the macroscopic scale, a potential-aware envelope encodes the external confinement, leaving the neural network to capture a smoother many-body residual. Across both two- and three-dimensional tests, the BINN approaches the Hartree and Gross-Pitaevskii limits with an empirical [MATH] finite-size trend in both energy and density. The energies agree with diffusion Monte Carlo to within [MATH] for the particle number tested up to [MATH] in the three-dimensional shrinking-range case. Applications are made under various trapping scenarios, justifying robust performance of BINN.
tldr: A symmetry-preserving boson-informed neural network computes ground states of interacting bosons via variational Monte Carlo with separated microscopic and macroscopic scales.
motivation: Accurate ground states of many-body Schrödinger equations are challenging due to the need to capture both short-range interaction and long-range confinement effects.
method: The BINN uses a cell Jastrow factor for near-contact stiffness, a potential-aware envelope for external confinement, and a neural network for the smoother many-body residual, trained variationally.
result: The method approaches Hartree and Gross-Pitaevskii limits, shows finite-size trends in energy and density, and agrees with diffusion Monte Carlo within stated accuracy for tested particle numbers in 3D shrinking-range cases.
conclusion: BINN provides robust performance under various trapping scenarios, offering a scalable neural-network approach for continuous-space bosonic ground states.

title: Two-Species Boltzmann--Kac Kinetics With Matsumoto--Yor Nonlinear Collisions: Conserved Energy And Conic Equilibria
authors: Yoshiaki Itoh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend Mark Kac's kinetic framework from single-species Euclidean spaces to a two-species, non-linear interaction space on the open cone [MATH] governed by the Matsumoto--Yor rational collision involution. We identify a non-linear conserved energy [MATH] and an invariant conic metric measure [MATH]. By establishing a two-species [MATH]-theorem, we prove that entropy production vanishes if and only if post-collision velocities are statistically independent ([MATH]). In contrast to the transform-domain proof of Letac and Weso{\l}owski~, which relies on joint Laplace transforms of general measures, our approach yields a direct physical derivation in state space via the transformation law for logarithmic gradients and separation of variables. This uncouples the functional-differential system to uniquely characterize the Generalized Inverse Gaussian (GIG) and Gamma distributions as the non-equilibrium thermodynamic equilibria.
tldr: The paper extends Kac's kinetic model to two-species nonlinear collisions on a cone, proves an H-theorem, and identifies GIG and Gamma distributions as non-equilibrium thermodynamic equilibria.
motivation: To generalize Kac's single-species kinetic framework to two-species systems with Matsumoto-Yor nonlinear collisions and characterize their thermodynamic equilibria.
method: Uses a direct state-space derivation via the transformation law for logarithmic gradients and separation of variables to establish a two-species H-theorem and an invariant conic measure.
result: Entropy production vanishes if and only if post-collision velocities are statistically independent; the Generalized Inverse Gaussian and Gamma distributions uniquely characterize the non-equilibrium thermodynamic equilibria.
conclusion: The work provides a physical derivation of equilibria for two-species Boltzmann-Kac kinetics, extending prior transform-domain results by Letac and Wesołowski.

title: Quantum-classical Algorithm Interpolation For Spatial Search
authors: Duarte Magano Diogo Ramos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum-walk algorithms can quadratically reduce the dependence of spatial search on the classical hitting time [MATH]. Realising this speedup using standard quantum-walk algorithms, however, requires deep coherent circuits, limiting their applicability on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices. We derive a parameterised family of hybrid quantum-classical spatial search algorithms that continuously interpolates between the classical and fully coherent quantum regimes, trading off circuit depth for total query complexity. For any [MATH], our algorithms use circuits of depth [MATH] and find a marked vertex with constant success probability at total cost [MATH], where [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] denote the setup, update, and checking costs, respectively. We also derive an optimal continuous depth-query trade-off for fixed-point amplitude amplification, providing a potential building block for other hybrid designs.
tldr: A parameterized family of hybrid quantum-classical algorithms interpolates between classical and quantum spatial search, trading circuit depth for query complexity.
motivation: Fully coherent quantum-walk spatial search requires deep circuits, limiting its applicability on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices.
method: The authors derive hybrid algorithms combining quantum walk steps with classical checking, parameterized by circuit depth, and analyze the depth-query trade-off, including fixed-point amplitude amplification.
result: For any depth, the algorithms find the marked vertex with constant success probability at total cost scaling with setup, update, and checking costs; an optimal continuous depth-query trade-off is derived for fixed-point amplitude amplification.
conclusion: This provides a flexible framework for quantum search on near-term devices and a potential building block for other hybrid quantum-classical designs.

title: Capacity Bounds For Optical Interference Channels Subject To Average Power Constraints
authors: Viswanathan Ramachandran
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate information-theoretic analysis of multiuser wavelength-division multiplexed (WDM) optical links is complicated by Kerr nonlinearity and chromatic dispersion. Existing capacity bounds for first-order regular perturbative (RP) channel models have relied on per-symbol peak power constraints to simplify the underlying extremal analysis. In this paper, we replace these peak constraints with the more practically relevant average input power constraints and study the resulting RP WDM interference channel. Unlike the peak-constrained formulation, an exact finite signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) analysis under average power leads in general to a nonconvex, high-dimensional optimization problem with no closed-form solution. We show that the problem admits a tractable characterization in the high-SNR regime. Using a genie-aided argument, we derive closed-form single-user high-SNR capacity bounds for the RP interference channel and identify constant-amplitude interferer signaling as extremal. Furthermore, under an empirically validated non-negativity condition on the dominant RP kernels and within a truncated first-order RP model, we establish a finite-SNR extremality result, yielding a single-user capacity characterization within the RP model under average power constraints. Building on these single-user corner points, we construct an all-helpsone achievable region via time sharing, which strictly improves upon treating nonlinear interference as noise. Numerical results and split-step Fourier simulations of the nonlinear Schrodinger equation channel confirm that the qualitative conclusions persist over practical launch powers. The results provide new insight into extremal signaling and multiuser trade-offs for nonlinear WDM systems within the RP approximation.
tldr: Derives capacity bounds for nonlinear optical WDM interference channels under average power constraints using regular perturbation models and high-SNR analysis.
motivation: Existing capacity bounds for perturbative optical WDM channels rely on per-symbol peak power constraints; average power constraints are more practically relevant but lead to nonconvex high-dimensional optimization.
method: Uses genie-aided arguments, high-SNR asymptotics, constant-amplitude interferer signaling, and a truncated first-order perturbation model to characterize single-user capacity and construct a time-sharing achievable region.
result: Obtains closed-form high-SNR single-user capacity bounds, a finite-SNR extremality result under a non-negativity condition, and an achievable region that strictly improves over treating nonlinear interference as noise; split-step Fourier simulations confirm the findings.
conclusion: Provides new insight into extremal signaling and multiuser trade-offs for nonlinear WDM systems within the regular perturbation approximation.

title: Efficient Construction Of Subspace Design Codes Over Constant Alphabet
authors: Shu Liu
