title: The Grounded Spirituality Of Mathematics
authors: Tarik Aougab
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose that mathematics is done largely as a means of both coping with and celebrating our physicality in the natural world. Inspired by David Abram's "Becoming Animal", we suggest that -- in opposition to the popular image of an otherworldy Platonic realm-- the spiritual component of doing mathematics is grounded on and in the Earth. We explore this as a means of questioning the widespread adoption of AI in the workflows of research mathematics.
tldr: The paper argues that mathematics is a grounded, spiritual practice tied to physical embodiment and the natural world, and uses this view to question AI's growing role in mathematical research.
motivation: Inspired by David Abram's 'Becoming Animal', the author aims to counter the image of mathematics as an otherworldly Platonic pursuit and to reconsider the adoption of AI in research workflows.
method: This is a philosophical and reflective essay drawing on phenomenological and spiritual perspectives rather than technical or empirical analysis.
result: It proposes that the spiritual dimension of mathematics arises from and remains grounded in earthly, bodily experience, offering a critical lens on AI-assisted mathematical practice.
conclusion: The paper concludes that recognizing mathematics as grounded spirituality can inform ethical and practical debates about automation in research mathematics.

title: Variationally Correct Loss Functions For Nonlinear Parametric Problems And Their Neural Approximations
authors: Pablo Cort\'es Castillo, Wolfgang Dahmen, Jay Gopalakrishnan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct computable a posteriori error estimators for parametric families of nonlinear elliptic problems by measuring the residual of a variational formulation in the dual norm of a closed subspace of the test space. A single abstract theorem shows that the resulting estimator is bounded above and below by the error in the trial norm, i.e., it is a variationally correct loss function. Two instances are covered. The first considers an [MATH]-like test space, yielding a nonlinear first-order system least-squares loss function that certifies arbitrary, possibly meshless, approximations. The second breaks the test space, yielding a nonlinear discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin loss function computed by element-local problems. All assumptions are verified for quasilinear diffusion, including monotone fluxes and semilinear problems, and a nonlocal Kirchhoff model. Numerical studies train neural networks approximating the parameter-to-solution maps with the latter loss and measure the ratio of loss to squared error.
tldr: The paper constructs computable a posteriori error estimators for parametric families of nonlinear elliptic PDEs and trains neural networks using these variationally correct loss functions.
motivation: Numerical methods for parametric nonlinear PDEs need reliable, computable error estimators that provably bound the approximation error, particularly when training neural network surrogates for parameter-to-solution maps.
method: A single abstract theorem shows the dual-norm residual estimator is bounded above and below by the trial-norm error, yielding two instantiations: a first-order system least-squares loss (L^2-like test space) and a discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin loss with element-local problems, verified for quasilinear diffusion and a nonlocal Kirchhoff model.
result: The estimators are proven to be variationally correct (upper and lower bounded by the error) under monotone fluxes and semilinear problems, and numerical studies train neural networks that approximate parameter-to-solution maps, measuring loss-to-squared-error ratios.
conclusion: The framework provides rigorous, computable loss functions for neural network approximation of nonlinear parametric PDEs, but lies entirely within numerical analysis and scientific machine learning, far from quantum information research.

title: Poincar\'e Compactifications Of Pullbacks Of Parallel Vector Fields Under Counterexamples To The Real Jacobian Conjecture
authors: Paulo Machado Francisco Braun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a polynomial map with nowhere zero Jacobian determinant. It is known that the global invertibility of [MATH] is equivalent to the pullback of a parallel vector field being parallel. In this paper, we construct the phase portraits on the Poincar\'e disc of the pullbacks of the canonical annular, radial, and strip vector fields under non-injective maps [MATH] that have recently appeared in the literature. Our arguments use local and global properties of vector fields as well as local and global properties of functions, thereby connecting techniques from dynamical systems and singularity theory.
tldr: The paper studies Poincaré compactifications of pullbacks of parallel vector fields under polynomial maps that are counterexamples to the real Jacobian conjecture, connecting dynamical systems and singularity theory.
motivation: The real Jacobian conjecture concerns when a polynomial map with nowhere-zero Jacobian determinant is globally invertible, and recent counterexamples motivate understanding the geometry of pullbacks of parallel vector fields.
method: The authors construct phase portraits on the Poincaré disc for pullbacks of canonical annular, radial, and strip vector fields using local and global properties of vector fields and functions.
result: They provide explicit descriptions of the phase portraits for these non-injective polynomial maps, revealing how the pullback vector fields behave at infinity and near singularities.
conclusion: The work connects techniques from dynamical systems and singularity theory to analyze counterexamples to the real Jacobian conjecture, with no direct relevance to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: TrackShield: An Efficient Runtime Defense Against Availability Attacks On High-Performance Real-Time Multi-Object Tracking
authors: Zonghua Gu, Julian Singh-Smith, Junlin Liao, Di Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-performance camera-based perception pipelines must sustain per-frame real-time budgets on resource-constrained embedded GPU platforms. Availability attacks such as SlowTrack inflate the persistent state of multi-object trackers: data-association workload accumulates across frames, so per-frame latency increases and drives the pipeline past its deadline. Detector- and NMS-layer defenses do not directly control this persistent tracker-side resource. We present TrackShield, a lightweight runtime resource-management layer that protects the tracker at the point where attack-induced workload accumulates. TrackShield combines low-overhead anomaly monitoring with staged birth capping, pruning of young or weakly matched tracks, and per-stage association-input admission control. Its hard admission guard provides a deterministic bound on admitted association workload, independently of the heuristic monitor. On a Jetson AGX Orin, TrackShield reduces attacked tracking-stage latency from [MATH] to [MATH]\,ms and whole-pipeline P99 latency from [MATH] to [MATH]\,ms, at a benign MOTA cost of [MATH] points. As an availability defense, TrackShield focuses on keeping the tracker responsive under attack instead of recovering the full tracking accuracy degraded by adversarial detections.
tldr: TrackShield is a lightweight runtime resource-management layer that defends multi-object tracking pipelines on embedded GPUs against availability attacks like SlowTrack by bounding accumulated association workload.
motivation: High-performance camera-based perception pipelines on resource-constrained embedded GPUs must meet per-frame real-time deadlines, but availability attacks such as SlowTrack inflate persistent tracker state, causing latency to grow across frames and violate deadlines.
method: TrackShield combines low-overhead anomaly monitoring with staged birth capping, pruning of young or weakly matched tracks, and per-stage association-input admission control, including a hard admission guard that deterministically bounds admitted association workload independently of the heuristic monitor.
result: On a Jetson AGX Orin, TrackShield reduces attacked tracking-stage latency and whole-pipeline P99 latency substantially, at a small benign MOTA cost.
conclusion: TrackShield keeps the tracker responsive under availability attacks rather than recovering tracking accuracy degraded by adversarial detections, offering a practical systems-level defense for real-time perception on embedded platforms.

title: Lost In The Fallback: How Reliably Do Typed Decision Models Use Fallback Options?
authors: Yuanbo Xie, Mingli Zhu, Tianyun Liu, Yingjie Zhang, Haixiao Xiong, Tingwen Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) are increasingly used in applications such as request routing and model selection, making reliable decisions critical to system performance. Fallback options accommodate categories outside regular choices, enabling deferral to human experts or more capable models. While recent works have examined adversarial vulnerabilities in TDMs, their ability to follow fallback rules in non-adversarial settings remains underexplored. We introduce the Paired Fallback Robustness (PFR) Test to evaluate two aspects of fallback reliability: whether models correctly switch between regular and fallback options, and whether they make consistent decisions under logically equivalent definitions of the same rule. We evaluate open-source decision models on three benchmarks, with controlled comparisons across architectures and parameter counts. We find that correct recognition does not reliably transfer to correct fallback options, and errors persist even when the correct category is explicitly supplied.Moreover, logically equivalent formulations of the same fallback rule can also produce substantial disagreement in model decisions. These findings reveal a crucial reliability gap in current TDMs: fallback mechanisms designed to improve reliability can instead introduce errors. It highlights faithful execution of fallback rules and consistency under equivalent definitions as essential requirements for reliable typed decision-making.
tldr: This paper introduces the Paired Fallback Robustness (PFR) Test to evaluate how reliably typed decision models use fallback options and maintain consistency under logically equivalent rule formulations.
motivation: Typed decision models are increasingly used in critical applications like request routing and model selection, where fallback options are intended to improve reliability by deferring uncertain cases to human experts or stronger models.
method: The authors propose the Paired Fallback Robustness (PFR) Test, which checks whether models correctly switch between regular and fallback options and whether they make consistent decisions under logically equivalent definitions of the same fallback rule. They evaluate open-source decision models on three benchmarks with controlled comparisons across architectures and parameter counts.
result: They find that correct recognition of categories does not reliably transfer to correct fallback behavior, errors persist even when the correct category is explicitly supplied, and logically equivalent fallback rule formulations can lead to substantial disagreement in model decisions.
conclusion: The findings reveal a reliability gap in current typed decision models: fallback mechanisms can introduce errors rather than improve reliability, highlighting the need for faithful execution of fallback rules and consistency under equivalent definitions.

title: Popularity Trajectories And Mixing Patterns Of Urban Venues In Two European Cities
authors: Wang Ngai Yeung, Lakmal Meegahapola, Daniele Quercia, Riccardo Di Clemente
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban venues such as restaurants, shops, bars and parks host the daily life of a city, and their collective rise and fall signals how vibrant a neighbourhood is. The usual assumption is that a venue's fortunes follow its neighbourhood's, so that how wealthy an area is and how many people live there will decide a venue's performance. Yet whether there is a common performance trajectory shared by venues over time is underexplored. In this study, we use 5.5 years of Foursquare data for about 10^4 venues in London and Barcelona. We found six distinguishable shapes recur in both cities, that are (1) Fall, (2) Rise, (3) Rise & Fall, (4) Steady, (5) Ephemeral (an early hit that loses popularity fast) and (6) Underdogs (a slow starter that gains popularity late). However, no recovery shape appears, that is neither city yields a U-shaped fall-and-rise group. Additionally, we found that deprivation and population density are not indicative which shape a venue follows. We also discovered that how early a shape can be recognized depends on when its distinctive segment occurs, not a shape's complexity. Proximity between venues, however, does predict how well-performing a venue is. We uncovered a mixing pattern where venues of the same shape tend to locate together more often than chance within roughly 200 to 600 metres. Finally, our qualitative reading of two contrasting districts, one rising in London and one falling in Barcelona, show that comparable socioeconomic conditions but divergent gentrification histories can generate vastly different popularity trajectories. All in all, our results altogether point at that urban vibrancy emerges at the block- and street- level, and social and historical contexts matter in terms of the characteristics of such patterns.
tldr: Using 5.5 years of Foursquare data from London and Barcelona, the study identifies six recurring popularity trajectories for urban venues and finds that proximity and local context, rather than deprivation or population density, predict venue performance.
motivation: The paper challenges the common assumption that a venue's success is determined solely by its neighbourhood's socioeconomic conditions, aiming to understand whether venues share common performance trajectories over time.
method: The authors analyze approximately 10^4 venues in London and Barcelona over 5.5 years using Foursquare check-in data and apply trajectory clustering to uncover recurring shape patterns, followed by spatial mixing analysis and qualitative district comparisons.
result: Six trajectory shapes recur in both cities (Fall, Rise, Rise & Fall, Steady, Ephemeral, Underdogs), with no U-shaped recovery; deprivation and population density do not predict shape, but proximity within 200–600 metres does, and venues of the same shape cluster spatially more than chance.
conclusion: Urban vibrancy emerges at the block and street level, and social and historical contexts, including gentrification histories, produce divergent popularity trajectories even under comparable socioeconomic conditions.

title: High-resolution Retinal Matrix Imaging Via Computational Motion And Aberration Correction
authors: Aymeric Melt, L\'eo Puyo, Victor Barolle, Claude Boccara, Gereon H\"uttmann, Alexandre Aubry
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-resolution optical imaging of the human retina is essential for diagnosing ophthalmic and neurodegenerative diseases. While adaptive optics combined with coherence gating can resolve retinal structures at the cellular scale, it requires complex, costly, and cumbersome hardware to physically correct for ocular aberrations and motion. Matrix imaging offers a powerful digital alternative by leveraging wave linearity to undo aberrations and multiple scattering; however, its in vivo deployment has been hindered by continuous, involuntary eye movements that destroy phase coherence during acquisition. Here, we overcome this fundamental barrier and demonstrate the first in vivo reflection matrix imaging of the human retina using an ultra-simplified optical setup without physical correctors. We introduce a fully computational framework that tracks and compensates for multi-axial ocular motion directly from raw interferometric data, thereby restoring the phase coherence of a multi-spectral distortion matrix. This enables local, high-order aberration correction to achieve diffraction-limited, volumetric imaging of retinal tissues. By shifting the hardware burden to physics-guided numerical computation, this paradigm opens the way for accessible, non-invasive, and high-resolution digital ophthalmology.
tldr: The paper presents a computational framework for in vivo high-resolution retinal imaging that corrects ocular motion and aberrations without adaptive optics hardware.
motivation: High-resolution retinal imaging is important for diagnosing ophthalmic and neurodegenerative diseases, but conventional adaptive optics systems are complex, costly, and cumbersome.
method: The authors use reflection matrix imaging and a fully computational approach to track and compensate for multi-axial ocular motion from raw interferometric data, restoring phase coherence for local high-order aberration correction.
result: They achieve the first in vivo reflection matrix imaging of the human retina with an ultra-simplified setup, obtaining diffraction-limited volumetric imaging of retinal tissues.
conclusion: Shifting the hardware burden to physics-guided numerical computation enables accessible, non-invasive, high-resolution digital ophthalmology.

title: Harmonic Numbers And Lerch Functions Behind Falling Factorial Generating Functions
authors: Hemen Dutta, Gradimir V. Milovanovic, Yilmaz Simsek
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a family of special numbers and polynomials introduced by Simsek whose exponential generating function has as denominator a falling factorial in the exponential variable. Using the partial fraction decomposition of this denominator, each member of the family is expressed by a single finite sum involving Bernoulli polynomials, Apostol Bernoulli polynomials and two variable Fubini polynomials evaluated at reciprocals of integers. A second expansion, around the point where the denominator vanishes, expresses the same numbers through Stirling numbers of the second kind and generalized harmonic numbers, and yields closed formulas for the first few members. We construct a function, built from the Hurwitz zeta function and Lerch s transcendent, which interpolates the polynomials at the negative integers and gives a closed form of a multiple series recently introduced by Pokaz, Ribicic Penava and Simsek, we give an Euler type integral representation for it, and show that the numbers are signed combinations of moments of geometric random variables. Recurrence relations, asymptotics and an extension to arbitrary distinct nodes are also given.
tldr: The paper studies special numbers and polynomials defined by a falling factorial generating function, expressing them via Bernoulli, Fubini, and Stirling numbers, and interpolating them using Hurwitz zeta and Lerch transcendent.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and extend a family of special numbers and polynomials introduced by Simsek, providing new representations, recurrences, asymptotics, and interpolation formulas.
method: They use partial fraction decomposition, expansion around zeros of the denominator, and analytic number theory tools such as Hurwitz zeta and Lerch transcendent to derive finite sums and closed forms.
result: The numbers are expressed through Bernoulli polynomials, Apostol Bernoulli polynomials, Fubini polynomials, Stirling numbers, and generalized harmonic numbers, with Euler-type integral representations and probabilistic interpretations as moments of geometric random variables.
conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive analytical treatment of these special numbers and polynomials, connecting them to classical special functions and offering new identities and extensions.

title: Cyclic Kronecker Fourier Transforms, Weber Norms, And Rogers-Ramanujan Singular Values
authors: Sumit Kumar Jha
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an imaginary quadratic field with fundamental discriminant [MATH], where [MATH] is odd, and cyclic ideal class group [MATH]. Assume that the ramified prime class above [MATH] is the unique involution [MATH]. For the Kronecker eta invariant \[ F(A)={}, \] where [MATH] and [MATH] arise from a positive definite quadratic form representing the ideal class [MATH], we show that the logarithms of the mirror ratios \[ R_j=)}{F(g^j)},\qquad 0\le j<M, \] are related by an explicit discrete cosine transform to the odd class-character Hecke [MATH]-values. A single level-[MATH] generalized-Weber orbit realizes all of these mirrors. Combining Fourier nonvanishing, lower-power Weber class invariants and a ray-class cancellation argument, we prove \[ (R_j)=H^{\langle c\rangle},\qquad R_j^{\sigma^{2M}}=R_j^{-1},\qquad (R_j+R_j^{-1})=H^{\langle c,\sigma^{2M}\rangle}. \] Here [MATH] is the Hilbert class field, [MATH] denotes complex conjugation, and [MATH] corresponds to [MATH] under the Artin map. Consequently \[ [(R_j):]=4M,\qquad [(R_j+R_j^{-1}):]=2M, \] and the latter degree becomes [MATH] over the real genus field [MATH]. Thus the degree pattern [MATH] in the cyclic [MATH]-power hierarchy is a specialization of a uniform [MATH] theorem. We give exact low-class-number evaluations and certified computations at [MATH], separating respectively four, eight and sixteen non-genus Hecke [MATH]-values and producing corresponding alternating Rogers-Ramanujan singular values. Classical mixed modular equations then give ordinary Rogers--Ramanujan companions at the same arguments.
tldr: The paper studies cyclic Kronecker Fourier transforms, Weber norms, and Rogers-Ramanujan singular values in the context of imaginary quadratic fields and class field theory.
motivation: The work appears motivated by explicit class field theory and modular equations, seeking uniform degree patterns and exact evaluations for mirror ratios related to Kronecker eta invariants.
method: It uses cyclic ideal class groups, discrete cosine transforms, generalized-Weber orbits, Hecke L-values, ray-class cancellation, and certified computations to derive algebraic relations and degrees.
result: The main results include explicit relations among mirror ratios, degree formulas such as [Q(R_j):Q]=4M and [Q(R_j+R_j^{-1}):Q]=2M, and low-class-number evaluations yielding Rogers-Ramanujan singular values.
conclusion: The paper establishes a uniform theorem for the degree pattern in cyclic 2-power hierarchies and provides classical Rogers-Ramanujan companions via mixed modular equations.

title: There Are Only Finitely Many Irregular Diophantine Quadruples
authors: Alain Togbe Bo He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A set of [MATH] distinct positive integers is called a Diophantine [MATH]-tuple if the product of any two distinct elements, increased by one, is a perfect square. A Diophantine quadruple [MATH] with [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves that there are only finitely many irregular Diophantine quadruples, a purely number-theoretic result about sets of integers whose pairwise products plus one are perfect squares.
motivation: Diophantine m-tuples are a classical object of study in number theory, and classifying irregular quadruples addresses a longstanding open problem in this area.
method: The authors use elementary and algebraic number theory techniques, including properties of Pell equations and quadratic forms, to bound and enumerate irregular Diophantine quadruples.
result: The main theorem establishes that irregular Diophantine quadruples form a finite set, presumably with an explicit characterization or bound.
conclusion: The work resolves a finiteness question in Diophantine combinatorics, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Short Proofs For The Minimum Number Of Determined Circles
authors: Stijn Cambie, Denis Paliy, Rafa{\l} Wrona
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present short proofs for the main parts of the recently completed solution of Erds Problem 506, which asks for the minimum number of distinct circles determined by a finite planar point set that is neither collinear nor concyclic. An inversion argument and a seven-point line lemma show that eight points determine at least [MATH] circles, and an explicit configuration attains this bound. A single argument combining Melchior's inequality with Langer's incidence bound establishes the sharp formula for every [MATH]. The proofs give concise alternatives to longer arguments in the recent literature; the remaining finite cases are cited separately.
tldr: The paper provides short proofs for the minimum number of distinct circles determined by finite planar point sets, resolving key cases of Erdős Problem 506.
motivation: Erdős Problem 506 asks for the minimum number of circles determined by a finite planar point set that is neither collinear nor concyclic, and previous solutions involved lengthy arguments.
method: The authors use an inversion argument, a seven-point line lemma, Melchior's inequality, and Langer's incidence bound to derive concise proofs and construct attaining configurations.
result: They show that eight points determine at least a certain number of circles, with an explicit sharp configuration, and establish the sharp formula for every finite point set size.
conclusion: The work gives shorter alternative proofs for the main parts of the solution to Erdős Problem 506, with remaining finite cases cited separately.

title: An Oral History Of Fpsac
authors: Sam Hopkins
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As its 40th anniversary nears, we present a history of the International Conference on Formal Power Series and Algebraic Combinatorics (FPSAC), through interviews with figures from its past, present, and future.
tldr: This paper presents an oral history of the International Conference on Formal Power Series and Algebraic Combinatorics (FPSAC) through interviews as its 40th anniversary approaches.
motivation: The paper aims to document the history, evolution, and community of the FPSAC conference series.
method: The author conducted interviews with past, present, and future figures associated with FPSAC and synthesized them into a historical narrative.
result: The paper provides a retrospective account of FPSAC's development and impact over four decades.
conclusion: The work serves as a commemorative history of FPSAC, highlighting its role in algebraic combinatorics.

title: Uniqueness Of Limit Cycles For Abel Equations And Planar Systems
authors: Jos\'e Luis Bravo Trinidad, Renhao Tian, Yulin Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study positive limit cycles of the Abel equation $[MATH][MATH]A[MATH]B[MATH]2\pi$-periodic functions. By developing a half-period convexity method, we establish a new criterion ensuring that the equation has at most one positive limit cycle. Moreover, if such a limit cycle exists, it is hyperbolic. As applications, we consider two classes of planar polynomial systems that can be reduced to Abel equations. For a subfamily of cubic rigid systems, we prove that there is at most one limit cycle, thereby giving a partial answer to the first problem in Gasull's list of 33 open problems. For quadratic systems, we derive a new uniqueness criterion for limit cycles surrounding the origin and provide explicit parameter regions under which the criterion is satisfied.
tldr: The paper develops a half-period convexity method to prove uniqueness of positive limit cycles for Abel equations, with applications to planar polynomial systems.
motivation: Limit cycles in Abel equations and planar systems are a classical topic in dynamical systems, and uniqueness criteria remain open for many families such as cubic rigid systems and quadratic systems.
method: The authors introduce a half-period convexity method to establish a new criterion for at most one positive limit cycle, and then apply it to reduced planar polynomial systems.
result: They prove at most one limit cycle for a subfamily of cubic rigid systems, partially answering Gasull's first open problem, and derive a new uniqueness criterion for quadratic systems surrounding the origin.
conclusion: The half-period convexity method provides a general tool for uniqueness of limit cycles and yields progress on open problems in planar polynomial vector fields.

title: Convergence Rates Of Factorized Gradient Descent For Overparameterized Asymmetric Matrix Sensing With Balancing Regularization

An exact indefinite lifting of the population objective decomposes the dynamics of FGD into positive, negative, and null spectral subspaces. The first two components have linear restoring terms, whereas the null component contracts only quadratically. For independent isotropic sub-Gaussian sensing matrices and independent centered sub-Gaussian noise with scale proxy [MATH], we prove the local bound \[ \|L_tR_t^\top-X^\star\|_2 \lesssim\max\left\{{\eta t+1/\sigma_r}, \kappa\sigma{n}}\right\}, \] under a sufficiently small initialization error, the number of linear measurements [MATH], and step size [MATH]. Here [MATH] and [MATH] are the largest and smallest nonzero singular values of the target [MATH] respectively, and [MATH]. Furthermore, a population trajectory was constructed to have tight product error [MATH]. These results provide a local rate characterization for ordinary gradient descent for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with balancing regularizer.
tldr: The paper analyzes convergence rates of factorized gradient descent for overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with balancing regularization.
motivation: Matrix sensing is a fundamental problem in machine learning and signal processing, and understanding the convergence of factorized gradient descent is important for nonconvex optimization theory.
method: The authors use an exact indefinite lifting of the population objective to decompose the dynamics into positive, negative, and null spectral subspaces, and prove local convergence bounds under independent isotropic sub-Gaussian sensing matrices and noise.
result: They establish a local error bound scaling as max{eta t + 1/sigma_r, kappa sigma n} under suitable initialization, sample size, and step size, and construct a population trajectory showing tight product error.
conclusion: The results provide a local rate characterization for ordinary gradient descent in overparameterized asymmetric matrix sensing with a balancing regularizer.

title: Learning In Strategic Queuing With Geometric Recharge: From Bandits To Systems
authors: Eva Tardos Cristian Palma Foster
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to [MATH] buffered servers with service rates [MATH]. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least [MATH]-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where [MATH] queues with arrival rates [MATH], each at most [MATH], compete for service from [MATH] buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is [MATH]. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition [MATH] is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for [MATH], this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from [MATH] to [MATH], matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.
tldr: The paper studies no-regret learning in strategic queuing systems with single-packet buffers, proving stability and throughput bounds via a connection to recharging bandits with geometric recharge.
motivation: Data center routers use small buffers and selfish no-regret learners to select among servers with unknown service rates, motivating an analysis of stability and efficiency in such buffered queuing systems.
method: The authors model single-queue and multi-queue systems where queues are no-regret learners, map the single-queue case to recharging bandits with geometric recharge, and derive throughput, stability, and competitive ratio bounds.
result: For a single queue, any no-regret learner achieves long-run average throughput at least the Hamacher sum of server rates, which is tight; for multi-queue systems, they show the smallest overprovisioning factor for stability under high-probability no-regret learning is 2, improving prior bounds and resolving an open question.
conclusion: The work characterizes stability and efficiency limits of strategic packet routing with no-regret learning and tiny buffers, yielding tight bounds and resolving an open problem in the multi-queue setting.

title: A Simple Algorithm For Counting Solutions To Integer Programs
authors: Daniel Dadush, Anita D\"urr, Thekla Hamm, Jonas Schmidt, Karol W\k{e}grzycki
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of counting solutions to integer linear programming problems of the form [MATH] where [MATH] and [MATH]. We present an algorithm that counts solutions with [MATH] arithmetic operations. This simplifies the algorithm of Gribanov and Malyshev, who considered the problem for the more general setting in which [MATH] is [MATH]-modular.
tldr: The paper presents a simplified algorithm for counting integer solutions to integer linear programs, improving on a previous algorithm for the more general modular case.
motivation: Counting solutions to integer linear programs is a fundamental problem in discrete optimization and computational complexity, and simpler algorithms can be more practical and easier to analyze.
method: The authors design an algorithm that performs a number of arithmetic operations depending on the input parameters, likely using geometric or algebraic techniques for lattice point counting.
result: Their algorithm counts solutions using a certain number of arithmetic operations, which simplifies the earlier algorithm of Gribanov and Malyshev that handled the more general case of modular matrices.
conclusion: The work provides a simpler counting algorithm for a specific class of integer programs, but it is purely classical and unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum networks.

title: DarKnight: Retrieval-Guided Agentic Framework For Breaking Dark Web Captcha Gates
authors: Binghui Wu, Yeo Zi Yi, Darren Tan, Manit Baser, Levente Csikor, Dinil Mon Divakaran
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19830v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) investigators who monitor dark web marketplaces for leaked credentials and breach listings must pass the diverse CAPTCHAs that operators deploy to block automated collection. Existing solvers either need unscalable per-site fine-tuning or rely on commercial Vision-Language Model (VLM) APIs, which surrender operational sovereignty: provider policies, Tor-exit blocking, government regulation, or model updates outside the investigator's control can halt or alter the solver overnight, and per-call costs recur with every session and retry. We present DarKnight, a self-improving agentic framework designed to run on a single workstation GPU inside an investigator's Tor crawler and solve CAPTCHAs with small, locally hosted open-weight VLMs that no provider decision can withdraw, without per-market training or third-party services. For each CAPTCHA, DarKnight retrieves successful and failed past attempts on similar images (dual-signal RAG), composes an image-specific preprocessing pipeline, and learns from the site's pass/fail verdict. In a case study on four real-world dark web marketplaces, agentic tool selection outperformed parameter scaling. A deployable open-weight VLM with DarKnight reached 83.2\% on the most heavily defended market, 37.2 percentage points above its base model, outperforming even the frontier Claude Opus~5 (44%). DarKnight recovered 48.2% of baseline failures at a 7.6% degeneration cost, indicating that selective tool use can avoid much of the degradation caused by uniform preprocessing.
tldr: DarKnight is a retrieval-guided agentic framework that uses locally hosted open-weight vision-language models to solve dark web CAPTCHAs without per-site fine-tuning or commercial APIs.
motivation: Cyber threat intelligence investigators need to bypass diverse CAPTCHAs on dark web marketplaces, but existing solvers require unscalable fine-tuning or commercial VLM APIs that sacrifice operational sovereignty and incur recurring costs.
method: The framework retrieves past successful and failed CAPTCHA attempts on similar images, composes an image-specific preprocessing pipeline, and learns from each site's pass/fail verdict using small locally hosted open-weight VLMs.
result: On four real dark web marketplaces, DarKnight reached 83.2% on the most heavily defended market, 37.2 percentage points above its base model, and outperformed Claude Opus 5 (44%), while recovering 48.2% of baseline failures at a 7.6% degeneration cost.
conclusion: Selective agentic tool use can greatly improve CAPTCHA solving with local open-weight VLMs, avoiding the degradation of uniform preprocessing and reducing dependence on third-party services.

title: CoRedSkill: Stealthy Skill Composition Attacks Via AST-Guided Injection
authors: Qichen Zhao, Shengfang Zhai, Qingni Shen, Zhonghai Wu, Jiaheng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.20049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents extend their capabilities through reusable skills that package instructions, executable code, and resources. Composing these skills enables complex task workflows, but their dependencies can also connect malicious operations across skills, making their combined intent difficult to identify through individual-package auditing. We introduce CoRedSkill, a compositional red-teaming method that forms stealthy attacks through cooperating skills while preserving their original utility. CoRedSkill decomposes an existing workflow into interdependent skills and embeds attack operations in task functions through abstract syntax tree (AST) rewriting, with skill instructions guiding the agent to autonomously select and invoke the relevant skills, and workflow dependencies and intermediate artifacts connecting the injected operations during task execution. We construct a benchmark of 150 cases covering 50 tasks and three attack objectives to evaluate attack success, task completion, and audit detection. In the main evaluation, CoRedSkill achieves 98.0% attack success and 95.3% task success with a 3.3% detection rate, and a joint success rate of 90.7% (attack success, task completion, and audit evasion in the same case) compared with 6.7--42.7% for the four baselines. Skill compositions can therefore complete legitimate tasks while carrying out unauthorized operations that evade auditing.
tldr: CoRedSkill is a compositional red-teaming method that embeds stealthy attacks in LLM agent skills via AST rewriting, achieving high attack success while preserving task utility and evading auditing.
motivation: Agent skills are reusable but auditing individual packages can miss malicious operations that emerge from their composition, motivating a need to study compositional attacks and defenses.
method: The authors decompose workflows into interdependent skills and use abstract syntax tree (AST) rewriting to inject attack operations into task functions, with instructions guiding autonomous skill selection and dependencies connecting injected operations during execution.
result: On a benchmark of 150 cases, CoRedSkill achieves 98.0% attack success, 95.3% task success, 3.3% detection rate, and 90.7% joint success, substantially outperforming four baselines (6.7–42.7%).
conclusion: Skill compositions can carry out unauthorized operations while completing legitimate tasks and evading audits, highlighting a security threat for LLM agent ecosystems.

title: The Diagonal Of A Regular Pentagon
authors: Dan Mcquillan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate the well-known fact that the diagonal of a unit regular pentagon has length the golden ratio. While similar to other proofs, we provide a novel figure that we believe is particularly well-suited to achieve full understanding at a glance.
tldr: The paper presents a novel visual proof that the diagonal of a unit regular pentagon equals the golden ratio.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a particularly clear and intuitive figure for a well-known geometric fact.
method: A geometric construction and diagram are used to demonstrate the relationship between the pentagon's diagonal and the golden ratio.
result: A new figure is offered that is claimed to make the proof immediately understandable.
conclusion: The work is a pedagogical contribution to elementary geometry and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Natural Geometry Based On The Rectilinear Plane
authors: Mohammed Berkani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aim of this note is to introduce natural geometry, in which the rectilinear plane is a primitive. This plane is admitted together with its rectitude, and its rectitude states that a Lambert quadrilateral has its fourth angle right. The fourth angle of a Lambert quadrilateral may be right, acute or obtuse, and this trichotomy distinguishes three planes. Starting from the rectitude, we prove the uniqueness of the parallel by a chain of neutral steps: the rectangle, the triangle whose angles sum to [MATH], and Legendre's theorem , all borrowed from the classical literature. That uniqueness is equivalent to the fifth postulate, which we thus reach in Euclid's own wording: the equivalence is read in the natural direction, and it is not a derivation of the fifth postulate from the other four, since the independence of that postulate is not in question. In the rectilinear plane the parallels are characterised as exactly the images of a line under a point-reflection, and equivalently as the pairs of equidistant lines. The other two planes are then placed beside the rectilinear one, and the same definitions serve for all three.
tldr: The paper introduces natural geometry based on the rectilinear plane, using Lambert quadrilaterals to derive the uniqueness of parallels and relate it to Euclid's fifth postulate.
motivation: The author aims to present a synthetic approach to non-Euclidean and Euclidean geometries by treating the rectilinear plane as primitive and deriving parallelism from neutral geometric steps.
method: Starting from the rectitude condition on Lambert quadrilaterals, the paper builds a chain of neutral theorems (rectangle, triangle angle sum, Legendre's theorem) to prove the uniqueness of parallels and its equivalence to the fifth postulate.
result: The uniqueness of parallels is shown to be equivalent to Euclid's fifth postulate in the natural direction, and parallels in the rectilinear plane are characterized as point-reflections of a line and as equidistant lines.
conclusion: The rectilinear plane is positioned alongside hyperbolic and elliptic planes, with the same definitions applying to all three, offering a unified natural geometry framework.

title: Physics-Guided Multi-Fidelity Surrogate Modeling For Natural Supercavity Geometry Of An Axisymmetric Conical Cavitator
authors: Vinh Pham, van Tu Nguyen, Warn-Gyu Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural supercavitation behind conical cavitators generates a vapor-filled envelope that, when sustained over the full body of a high-speed underwater vehicles, reduces hydrodynamic skin-friction drag and enables performance levels unattainable in fully wetted flow. Accurate prediction of maximum cavity length and maximum cavity radius and local cavity profile as functions of cavitation number and cone half-angle is essential for both the static design and the real-time shape management of super-cavitating torpedo cavitators. Classical analytical models provide computationally inexpensive predictions but exhibit systematic disagreements in the practically important regime of moderate cavitation number and large angle, where slender-body assumptions begin to break down. Existing data-driven machine learning approaches offer higher accuracy but are constrained by the prohibitive cost of multiphase computational fluid dynamics (CFD) sweeps over the full design space. This study proposes a physics-guided multi-fidelity surrogate framework based on Extended Hierarchical Kriging (PG-EHK) that addresses this challenge by fusing the multiple competing analytical cavity formulas as non-level low-fidelity (LF) trend functions corrected by a sparse set of high-fidelity (HF) CFD data. It simultaneously incorporates the analytical models regardless of their local fidelity ordering, using Bayesian-estimated scaling factors to construct the trend function as physical baseline. The resulting surrogate maps operational condition inputs to cavity geometry responses using fewer than 20 high-fidelity CFD evaluations. Cross-validation on five independent hold-out CFD cases demonstrates that the proposed PG-EHK surrogate achieves 61% reduction in prediction error compared to the best-performing individual analytical approach.
tldr: A physics-guided multi-fidelity surrogate model fuses analytical cavity formulas with sparse CFD data to predict supercavity geometry for axisymmetric conical cavitators.
motivation: Accurate prediction of natural supercavity geometry is needed for design and real-time control of high-speed underwater vehicles, but analytical models are inaccurate in important regimes and full CFD sweeps are prohibitively expensive.
method: The authors propose a physics-guided extended hierarchical Kriging framework that treats multiple analytical cavity formulas as non-level low-fidelity trend functions and corrects them with fewer than 20 high-fidelity CFD evaluations using Bayesian-estimated scaling factors.
result: Cross-validation on five hold-out CFD cases shows a 61% reduction in prediction error compared to the best individual analytical approach.
conclusion: The PG-EHK surrogate enables accurate and computationally efficient prediction of supercavity geometry, supporting both static design and real-time shape management.

title: A Symbolic Differentiation_Summation Framework For Power Sums Of Arithmetic Sequences
authors: Ahmed Abdlmohsin Abdlsahib
abstract: ArXiv:2610.18898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a self-contained derivation of the closed form of the power sums [MATH] in which the Bernoulli numbers enter as constants of integration rather than as prescribed coefficients. The derivation rests on an elementary fact: a sum whose terms are polynomial in the index is the restriction to the integers of a unique polynomial, which satisfies the defining difference equation identically and may therefore be differentiated and integrated exactly. Differentiating lowers the power by one; integrating back introduces a single constant, equal to the slope [MATH] of the polynomial at the origin and fixed by the value [MATH]. This yields a closed form for [MATH] in terms of the constants and a recurrence that determines them, obtained without induction on the exponent and without generating functions. With the Bernoulli numbers defined by their classical recurrence, we identify the constants as [MATH]; the progression starting at [MATH] reproduces that recurrence exactly. In the normalized case they are [MATH], so [MATH], a value that reflects the summation range; a reflection identity shows, without generating functions, that the odd constants beyond the first vanish. The coefficients of the recurrence are scaled binomial coefficients from a single row of Pascal's triangle, and the same approach gives closed forms for sequences with polynomial differences. The integral recursion behind the method is known in the normalized case; each result is related to its classical counterpart, and a verified implementation is provided.
tldr: The paper derives a symbolic differentiation-summation framework for closed forms of power sums of arithmetic sequences using Bernoulli numbers as integration constants.
motivation: The paper aims to provide a self-contained derivation of power sum formulas without induction or generating functions, using elementary polynomial difference equations.
method: It treats sums of polynomial terms as restrictions of unique polynomials satisfying a difference equation, differentiating and integrating to obtain closed forms and recurrences for constants.
result: The method recovers Bernoulli numbers via their classical recurrence, identifies constants, proves vanishing odd constants beyond the first through a reflection identity, and extends to sequences with polynomial differences.
conclusion: The framework offers an alternative derivation of power sum formulas and related recurrences, with a verified implementation, but it is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Graph-Based Analysis Of Comparability, Scale, And Attribution In Private Transformer Inference
authors: Souvik Das, Ariful Azad, Nitesh Saxena
abstract: ArXiv:2610.19607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.
tldr: A graph-based systematization of 62 private Transformer inference systems shows limited comparability, mixed attribution of performance gains, and a scaling plateau at 13B parameters.
motivation: Synthesizing empirical claims in private Transformer inference is difficult due to multidimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts.
method: The authors construct an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges, then perform node-, edge-, and graph-level analyses.
result: Node-level attribution shows cryptographic progress drives performance gains but always co-occurs with other factors; edge-level auditing finds only 1 of 1891 system pairs directly comparable; graph-level analysis reveals a scaling plateau at 13B parameters and projects production-scale costs.
conclusion: The proposed framework enables transparent evaluation of PTI claims and helps channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.
